analysis.one_liner: Lifts the Social Security payroll tax cap so all earnings are taxed, and increases retiree benefits.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by Sen. Tom Harkin with 4 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in March 2013 and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would apply the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax to every dollar of wages and self-employment income, phased in from 2014 to full coverage by 2018 — under current law, wages above roughly $113,000 a year are exempt. The new revenue would help pay for higher benefits: a boost to the benefit formula that helps lower and middle earners most, and annual cost-of-living increases based on a new inflation index reflecting what retirees actually buy. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries. The bill raises the first tier of the benefit formula (up to 15% higher by 2033), counts a share of high earners' above-cap income toward benefits, and switches annual cost-of-living adjustments to a new retiree-specific inflation index [S2][S3]. The new payroll tax revenue would also extend the program's financing.

how_it_helps.text: Phases in the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax on earnings above the annual wage cap, starting with 20% of above-cap income taxed in 2014 and rising each year until all of it is taxed in 2018 [S3].

Raises the first bend point of the benefit formula by 1 percentage point per year from 2019 through 2032, reaching 15% above the current formula in 2033 and after — a change that raises benefits proportionally most for lower-earning retirees [S3].
Counts 5% of a worker's earnings above the wage cap toward their benefit calculation, so high earners receive some additional credit for the new taxes they pay [S3].

Directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish a Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, tracking the spending of people at retirement age, and uses it to compute Social Security cost-of-living increases — an index that historically rises slightly faster than the one currently used [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Individuals with earnings above the Social Security wage cap (about $113,700 in 2013) and the employers of those workers, who together pay the 12.4% payroll tax on income that is currently exempt. Self-employed high earners pay both halves [S3].

drawbacks.text: High earners would pay the payroll tax on income above the cap while only 5% of that income counts toward their future benefits, weakening the traditional link between what top earners pay in and what they get out [S3].
Employers pay half of the tax on the newly covered wages, so businesses with many highly paid employees face a new payroll cost, and self-employed high earners bear the full 12.4% on their own [S3].

The benefit improvements phase in slowly — the bend point increase starts only for people becoming eligible after 2018 — while the tax phase-in begins in 2014, so the bill collects revenue years before most beneficiaries see larger checks [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a substantial tax increase on the highest earners for higher benefits and stronger financing for a program tens of millions of retirees depend on. The design is progressive: the benefit-formula change lifts lower and middle benefits proportionally more than high ones. The main honest costs are the new 12.4% tax burden on all high-wage earnings (with only partial benefit credit), the added payroll cost for employers of high earners, and the slow phase-in of the benefit gains.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in March 2013 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin introduced the bill on March 14, 2013; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day [S1][S5].
Four Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4].
The action history shows no further action after the referral — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the wage cap and their employers are better off because the bill died — they avoided a phased-in payroll tax on all earnings. Meanwhile, the solvency and benefit improvements it proposed were never enacted, leaving Social Security's financing shortfall unaddressed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the payroll cap

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 14, 2013 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended [S1][S5].

sides.party_line_note: All five senators behind the bill — the sponsor and four cosponsors — were Democrats, and the bill never reached a floor vote, so there are no roll calls showing how anyone else would have voted [S1][S4].

industries.industry: High earners above the Social Security wage cap
industries.note: Their earnings above the cap (about $113,700 in 2013) become subject to the 12.4% Social Security tax, phased in to full coverage by 2018, while only 5% of that income counts toward their own future benefits [S3].
Employers pay half of the payroll tax on wages that were previously exempt above the cap, a new cost on high-payroll businesses [S3].
